utterances.text: Looking at the text of this document, I will just have you confirm that concern was expressed in paragraph 3 about helicopter flights.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry Ms. Bolton was there a question? I missed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, just -- I'm going to ask the question now: Is this the --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- helicopter flights that we have been speaking about up to this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were those flights, do you recall, investigated? The allegation about the flights?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There seemed to be an investigation that went beyond just kind of a normal glossing over. What I mean by that is the question was asked why, in fact, were not the observers allowed to be at their posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will return to that in a moment. And could I just have you look at the first numbered paragraph on page 2. We had seen in the text previously that Mr. Djokic had been calling for elimination of all sanctions. What did the United Nations in fact do with respect to the sanctions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They remained in place by and large.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And looking at paragraph 1, it would appear that the suspensions that were -- or partial suspensions that was already in place was to continue in effect until 5th, July, 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, more or less the status quo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could turn to the next document in that same tab. You should have 65 ter 6076. And we have reproduced pages 1 to 7 only without the annexes, and this document is on the letterhead of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia with a title inquiry into unexplained radar traces. Have you had the opportunity at any point in time, sir, to read this report?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The substance of it is familiar. Honestly, I cannot recall whether I have actually seen the report itself. But the substance is very much familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you about some of the passages then and can you indicate whether you can or are -- or are not in a position to answer. Do you recall -- I'm look specifically at the findings section which is the very last page, page 4, number page 4 on the bottom, where the signatures of five individuals occur?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. The first paragraph they're talking about the radar systems capabilities at someplace called Surcin or Surcin airport. Where is that airport, in what country?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The FRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did the mission have its own radar facilities to assist in monitoring the border?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, there was no -- no such capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was there any equipment available to monitor the border within the borders of -- for -- sorry, sir, let me strike that. Let me move on, sir, just to the last -- 17 and 18 talk about the unexplained traces that they call it and use the words "give rise to suspicion." And they characterize the incident of 6 April 1995 as highly suspicious. Ultimately, are they able to make any other finding other than characterizing it as highly suspicious?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is actually a mischaracterization of the findings.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm quoting from paragraph 18. The incident on 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say ultimately. Fine, I leave it for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thought you were referring to the findings in their entirety. I withdraw what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, I will rephrase my question. The finding in paragraph 18 is that there were no other information available to prove that any of the unexplained radar traces were helicopters crossing the border: "However, the incident on 6 April 1995 was considered highly suspicious." Is that -- does that accord with your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. You asked me if there were any other sources of -- for this type of radar information. I would just like to highlight that there may have been other nation states that had their own access. Of course, I was not privy to that nor do I know if, in fact, the monitoring mission was privy to that. So there may have been input beyond the scope that I'm aware of here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The paragraph I'm most interested in, sir, is the next paragraph, paragraph 19. Which reads: "The ICFY monitor mission, particularly at its current manning level, does not have the compatibility to monitor effectively the closure of the air border." Did that situation change at all in the wake of this report?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, as -- less than a month later, I would receive information of Serbian forces crossing the border. This information came, as far as I know, from national sources. I'm not sure if it was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you handing over to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't have a connection anymore. Do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could try reconnecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think Madam Registrar is trying that. Let's see.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Ms. Bolton can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, we seem to have re-established contact, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I don't know when my answer was cut off, but very briefly, within a month, less than a month of this date, I did receive information from other sources, national sources; in this case, the government of the Netherlands, the defence minister, who had received information that there were military personnel and goods coming in from Serbia and Montenegro. Whether this information was available to the United Nations Monitoring Mission, or whether, in fact, it came itself from the UN Monitoring Mission, I'm is it not sure. Subsequent, I only heard rumours, and again they are rumours, that they came from central intelligence sources. So that is my best answer to your question right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If this could be marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have no objection to it at all. I would suggest the entirety of the document go. I understand it is only a partial document, but since the findings are predicated upon the annexes, it would make sense that the Chamber has available to it the specific information contained in the annexes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can I tell that you the witness doesn't have the annexes available to him, certainly in paper form, so I would just ask that the document, as it appears for now, be marked as an exhibit. And if my friend has -- wishes in cross-examination to refer to the annexes, he can make those materials available to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say the document as it appears in its entirety or only the pages that you referred to at the beginning of this --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just pages 1 to 7 which is what the witness has in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think there any dispute between the parties that the balance of the document and the appendixes that were forwarded to the Defence by the Prosecution are, in fact, an accurate reflection of what the document, in its entirety, is. If need be, I will figure a way of uploading the balance of the document and showing him each and every page thereafter. But that doesn't seem to be a particularly good use of time and under the doctrine of complete principle, it would make sense for the entire document to go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But we do have guidelines which suggest that if the entire document is not being used, we must just admit those pages that are being used. I think, therefore, that if we admit what Madam Bolton is tendering, we will also add to that exhibit what you may raise from the rest of the documents during your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The difficulty that I have with -- with the proposed method of accepting this exhibit is as follows: The report findings in analysis are based upon hard data which is attached to the report. When the witness is responding to the report's findings and the -- and other information that's contained within the first seven pages that is necessarily including the annexes. So in fact, the witness is, if not directly, certainly indirectly, dealing with those particular pages. I mean, it seems to me to be a sensible way of doing it. As I said earlier, under the doctrine of completeness, that way the Chamber has before it, the entire document, has the witness's responses to the entire document, and is in a position to objectively, rationally, and reasonably deal with the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I don't see how -- where the witness refers to annexes, number one. I don't know how many pages this constitutes. And unless I know the number of pages, I don't think I can accede to this request. Seventy-three pages, when only seven pages have been used. I would suggest that -- I rule that, in fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We accept what is tendered and whatever else comes to [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I asked to be marked for identification, at this time ... [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If could you allow me to finish to speak, Mr. Guy-Smith, we will then go quicker. If you interrupt me, then we won't finish. I was saying, I think we should admit the seven pages, and any additional pages that come later, can be admitted into the same exhibit as and when they are tendered at that time. I don't think it is prudent out of the 73-page document where only seven pages are being used to admit an entire 73 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand what you said, Your Honour, and I thank you for the opportunity to have this particular exhibit become a complete exhibit under a doctrine, which I think is fundamental to a fair determination. And I would point out to the Court that at a point in time when this case finally comes to you, you will find there are many, many, many documents in which the number of pages that have been used, as opposed to the number of pages which have been admitted are the difference between chalk and cheese.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I repeat my ruling by reference. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: First seven pages of 65 ter 6076 will become Exhibit P2485.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, if could you turn to tab 10 in the binder before you. You should have 65 ter 9057 before you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's a letter from the 19th May, 1995, permanent representative of Croatia, where the permanent representative writes: "Following the restoration of the Croatian authority in the Western Slavonia region, I should like to inform you that the law enforcement authorities of the Republic of Croatia have discovered payroll lists of officers commissioned in the Army of Yugoslavia that have been detached on active duty to the occupied territories of Croatia. The 18th Corps of the so-called Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Okucani (unit identification number 9162) has consistently forwarded its payroll lists to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia in Belgrade." And the next paragraph starts -- says: "The said list include the name of" -- and then there's a series of names, and ends with the words, "This is but a small sample of Yugoslav commissioned officers." Could you confirm whether you received a copy of this letter in 18th May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, my screen has lost the connection again. Is that true for everyone?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Second time it has dropped. But the [indiscernible] is back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are back.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear your question, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You didn't hear the question at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did hear your question, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you confirm whether you received this letter then?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2486, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In that same tab, sir, if you would skip forward one document, you should find a document, 65 ter 9051. It's a telefax message page it starts with?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And it should be a letter dated 28th June, 1995, from the Republic of Croatia, addressed to the then Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not this document - and take a moment to review it, if you need to - was circulated to yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I should remind you, at that time, that I had taken over the post of the foreign minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I may not have been, at that time, present in New York nor receiving them directly, but I am aware of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. How did you become aware of it; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Almost any document that came to the United Nations still ultimately was forwarded to me. What I cannot necessarily tell whether it was forwarded as a document of the Security Council or a document of the United Nations Secretary-General's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And what would the difference be in terms of whether particularly a copy would have been given to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be a document, generally a short introductory page saying that this document is being circulated as a document of either the Security Council or General Assembly or the Secretary General's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you on the same page as the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I think I need to clarify that point with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry sir. Is there any means of telling if this was document was or was not circulated to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I find on the front page is it says: "Please find attached a letter of Mr. Granic sent to Secretary-General of UN on June 28, 1995." That does not necessarily mean that, in fact, it would have been circulated as a document of the United Nations or the Secretary-General's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not copies would have gone to the members of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be very likely. In fact, I would feel very comfortable in saying yes, but I cannot be 100 percent sure on the basis of the document that I see in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be tendered as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2487.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This next document, sir, is -- should be found at tab 10 as well. And should be the second-last document in that tab, a meeting of the Security Council, July 5th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, the 65 ter number is 8862.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I don't wish to go into much detail about this, sir, other than to have you confirm that this document is a true record of the proceedings that date?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be tendered as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2488.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Again, sir, would you just confirm that the subject of discussion at that meeting was what should happen with the partial suspension of the sanctions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And on that occasion, I'm going to suggest that you spoke, the Croatian representative spoke, and Mr. Djokic spoke.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And if you would just turn to the last document in that tab, you should have Defence Exhibit 28. And that should be Resolution 1003, 5th July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The Security Council includes, on the first page, the language: "Underlining the particular importance it attaches to there being no provision of military assistance, in terms of finance, equipment, coordinates or air defences or recruitment of troops to the Bosnian Serb forces." And then goes on, on the next page, at paragraph 1 to decide that the restrictions and other measures referred to in paragraph 1 of Resolution 943 shall be suspended until 18th September, 1995. You were, at this time, I think -- did you indicate foreign minister at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Were you -- I take it you would not then have been present at the -- well, no, sorry you were present at this session because you gave a speech. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recall -- do you recall the conversation or the discussion around the inclusion of the language where the Security Council talks about the importance of there being no provision of military assistance, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. And it was a special concern, because a month earlier, I had receive reports of Serbian forces from Serbia and Montenegro amassing around Srebrenica. I'm referring to the intelligence source that I just mentioned a few minutes earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm unclear as to which intelligence source that is. At one point, he said central intelligence, at another point, he mentioned the Pentagon. I'm not sure. Is he talking about something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm clear, but I'll -- I have no difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The person or person who is first told you about troops amassing in the area around Srebrenica, do you recall who that was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Defence Minister Voorhoeve, of the Netherlands, and we had met during a meeting of the peacekeeping countries in Paris at the very end of May /beginning of June. It was a two-day meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that accommodation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reference to the CIA was what his sources of information may have been and only subsequent to that, and very long time later, did someone mention that that was his source. So I apologise for any confusion to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. The remaining sanctions against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, do you recall at what point in time it was that those remaining -- the bulk of the sanctions were actually lifted?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bolton, there were several steps to be pursued in conjunction with the signing and adoption and implementation of the Dayton Agreement, including, in particular, the issue of mutual recognition.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So am I understanding you correctly that it was only after there was recognition and the signing of the Dayton Accord that these sanctions were lifted?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The [indiscernible] of mutual recognition was the most critical point. That is correct, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could I just have you identify, for the purpose of record, the document at tab 32, which is 65 ter 6781.01, Resolution 1022?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Is that the resolution affected or set out the conditions and timing of the lifting of the remaining sanctions that you've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is. I believe it was something that was discussed in -- ahead of time in Dayton as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P2489.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I wish to now move forward, thankfully, to 1995. There's going to be four topics I'm going to discuss with you in respect of 1995. First topic is going to be Sarajevo; second topic is going to be Zagreb; the third topic will be Srebrenica; and briefly we will touch on Dayton, okay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. We have talked about, in respect of Sarajevo, the situation through 1994 up until the fall, and you have told us in your testimony to date, that in the fall of 1994 or late -- I think you said late summer that the cease-fire had fallen apart and that there was renewed shell and sniper attacks. Could you -- from the fall of 1994 or late summer 1994 through to the end of war, was there any landing cease-fire in respect of Sarajevo at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You told us earlier in your evidence that you had occasion to visit Sarajevo during the war. Approximately how many times did you visit the city?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say approximately ten. In particular, during the latter part of the war, 1994/1995, I was there more frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And why is it that you were there more frequently at that point?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number one my responsibilities had expanded, as just in consistent with my duties as ambassador to the UN, agent before the International Court of Justice, working with the war crimes tribunal. But when I became foreign minister, then I think I should be clear, I was in Sarajevo in and out constantly; and, therefore, that number ten would be, by far, much higher. So let me please correct my answer. Until the time I became foreign minister, which was at the very end of May, I had visited Sarajevo approximately ten times. After that, it was almost constant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just want to ask you very briefly about your personal experiences an observations, in terms of shelling. And to do that, I want to refer you to a couple of documents. Tab 8 in the binder you have before you. You should find a letter, 65 ter number 8850?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the document number, Ms. Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Tab 8 is where I think you should find it as the first document.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. We have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Is this a letter that you wrote, sir, dated 9th May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And this was a letter addressed to the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you describe in this letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described the particular incident where I was supposed to come into Sarajevo and to receive the benefit of the protection of the United Nations Protection Force. As we were coming in over Mount Igman, there was intensive fire that seemed to anticipate my arrival and the arrival of what, then, was Vice-President Ejup Ganic. The UN force, subsequently, informed my team that was coming in, that, in fact, they were too concerned - I don't want to use the work afraid - but too concerned about the fire, and that they did not wish to risk their personnel, to send up an armoured personnel carrier to Sarajevo -- to send an armoured personnel carrier from Sarajevo to Mount Igman. At that point in time, because of the urgency of the matters I got out of the vehicle and came down on foot, down Mount Igman, at which time there continued to be firing and shelling upon our position; and, unfortunately, in one rather memorable moment, a shell came over our heads and landed just on the other side of a hill, and, as we found out later, had hit an innocent woman who was up in the mountains gathering wood and who had the side of her torso, in effect, torn apart. Unfortunately, the woman did not survive. Obviously I faired better, and moved down the mountain, moved down foot into -- toward the tunnel and came through the tunnel into Sarajevo. That personal experience, though, had a much broader relevance which was that, in fact, the United Nations -- the United Nations Protection Force was not able to control the entry of personnel, including diplomatic personnel such as myself, but most importantly of goods and even of its own personnel. In fact, the United Nations by then had --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, you're getting off topic on me.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My question, with respect to this incident, sir, was: Were there any military personnel as part of your convoy or accompaniment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Any military targets in the vicinity in which you were travelling?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2490.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I want to refer to you a second document at tab 11. If you would just turn forward, please, you should have 65 ter 8861.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And that should be a letter, 27th June, 1995, from your charge d'affaires to which was annexed a letter from yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I just have you confirm, sir, that you authored this letter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And does it accurately reflect the observations that you were making at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. In the context of what was supposed to be the exclusion zone of Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May be it please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2491.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, sir, if you could turn back to tab 8, again, please. You should have a series --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're there, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. A series of four documents that starts with 65 ter 8851, which is a letter dated 12th May 1995. And with respect to the subsequent document, you should have 65 ter 8852; 65 ter 8853, which is a letter dated 24th May 1995? Do you have those three documents, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect to each of these documents, could you simply confirm the authenticity of these documents, that they are, in fact, letters written either by yourself or the persons cited in the letters?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And, again, sir, each of these documents indicates the request that they be circulated as documents either of both the General Assembly and Security Council or the Security Council. To the best of your knowledge were they so circulated?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And generally each of these letters pertains to events in Sarajevo; is that fair, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could each of those documents be introduced into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I certainly don't have a problem with that. I don't know whether or not the Chamber has had an opportunity to see them all. The only one I see on the screen is the -- I believe the first one, which is 65 ter 8851.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the meantime, can we accept 8851 into evidence and give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2492.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have we now seen 8852 on the screen? Is that it, that we see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't know ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is anybody able to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That is the document, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit P2493, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we now see 8853. Is that it? Thank you. May it please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit P2494, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The last document in that tab, sir, should be a letter dated 1st June 1995, 65 ter 88 -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Brief indulgence [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Registrar, I think I've given you the wrong 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is 0885.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] For the 1st of June, Ms. Bolton, I have here 08858.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, that is actually not the document I wanted; sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could flip back in that tab, sir, to 65 ter 8856, should be a letter dated 30th May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We could display it electronically, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you prefer, Ms. Bolton, I'll be fine with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could ask the Registrar here to do that, if she can, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we have it, according to the Registrar in front of me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Dated 30th of May, 1995, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I having problems? I don't seem to see a date -- I see a letter that says --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour is right. I'm looking at the date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That should be a letter annexed, in the annex from Hasan Muratovic and he, in his letter, describes some conditions in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, if you can look at the contents of that letter and just confirm for me whether or not that information, to the best of your knowledge, accurately reflects the situation in Sarajevo at the time of the writing of that letter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P2495.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do we have the capabilities of going into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, we do have the capability.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session. Do you want closed session or private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, if we could ask the witness, please, to turn to tab 7 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Should have before you document 65 ter 1436. It should be a translation of an article from a newspaper or publication called "Argument." Are you familiar with that publication, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaguely, I am, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. This is a document dated 24th March, 1995, which purports to be a subject interview with General Milan Celeketic. And in the article, looking at the first page, is an indication that General Celeketic is quoted as having said, "If attacked, we will target the squares of large cities." My question is: Had you ever seen this or heard that quote -- or seen this article or heard this quote before today?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I would like to emphasise I have not read the article. I have -- the contents of this were very familiar to me, and I had discuss it with my colleagues back then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did ask you a compound question there. I take it you were familiar with the quote but not the article. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the associates or persons that you discussed it with at that time, who would that have been?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been people within my own mission, that is the mission of mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the mission of Croatia as well and others within the United Nations's framework.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that this document be tendered into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do not believe there has been a relationship made between this document and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you say that again, Mr. Guy-Smith? I didn't hear the first word.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do not believe that there has been a relationship been made between this document and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm content that it be marked for identification purposes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May it be admitted into evidence, and marked for identification. May it please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document will become Exhibit P2497, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The second document in tab 7, sir, if you would turn to it should be Defence Exhibit D5.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: 4th May, 1995, Security Council document?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And if you would confirm for me, sir, that this is -- just looking, sorry, at the fourth quoted paragraph there, where the Security Council also condemns the bombardment of Zagreb. Do you see that text, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My screen still shows the Celeketic thing. Is it possible to see this document that is being discussed?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. It's D5; I'm sorry, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, we now have it displayed in the courtroom. Can you just confirm for me whether this is an authentic copy of statement that was released to the Security Council, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on how much attention in the media the shelling of Zagreb attracted?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a bit as it -- as, obviously, it seemed like a re-escalation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm finished with this document, and I would be moving on a different subject area. Do you wish me to continue going or do you wish to take a break? The next subject area is Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... but if this is convenient for you, we'll take a break. Can I just that can he take a break of about 15 minutes to 20 past and then come back and sit for 40 minutes. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the record show that we now sit as a full Bench, with Judge David having joined us, no longer pursuant to 15 bis. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I want to change -- or start now to discuss the events surrounding Srebrenica in 1995. Could you tell me what you understood, based on the information you were receiving, and you have already touched on this, what the humanitarian situation was, within the Srebrenica safe area in the spring of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bolton. I had generally three sources of information. One is the United Nations; the second is my government, or direct sources there; and the third is actually the Dutch government, which was also interacting with its own forces. There were several simultaneous events developing. One of them that seemed to be of most immediate concern is that the safe area, itself, seemed to be shrinking. The Dutch, as other UN protection forces had done in the past, had established outposts to observe and, of course, to be able to trigger response to any attack on the safe area itself. So it seemed that some of those outposts were first under attack and then some, in fact, were either overrun or had to be abandoned. Number 2, the Dutch forces, themselves, were actually under severe humanitarian conditions. They were only given enough food and medicines to cover themselves. They only had enough -- at best limited fuel supplies. They were not able, in any way, to share any of what they received with the local population, which in some instances actually put them into a rather uncomfortable -- I don't want to say at adversarial position, but certainly would initiate conflicts, because the Dutch, at least, had enough to survive while the local population did not. In addition to a lack of food, lack of medicines, and I emphasise those because there were specific discussions on those points with the Dutch government, particularly Defence Minister Voorhoeve. There was also apparently a lack of iodine, which we were able to confirm, which produced its own unique health results, both physical and even psychological. We understood, coming now in the late spring of 1995, that the situation was of the most dire nature, that we were dealing with potential deaths. We were certainly dealing with long-term effects upon the health of this population. We were dealing with potential conflict that could arise with the haves and the have not's, if I can use that term, that is the peacekeepers versus the local population. And the Dutch forces, themselves, obviously were suffering under very severe conditions and their ability to perform their mission was impeded. I hope that suffices for your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If the UN resolutions had been fully abided by, should there have been any difficulty in humanitarian aid reaching the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. And the attack on the -- on the UN outpost itself was just another element of non-compliance as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was preventing humanitarian aid, or who or what was preventing humanitarian from reaching inside Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we understood, there, in fact, was a very deliberate strategy to deny both the local population that, of course, included many displaced persons and refugees, but also even to deny the Dutch forces themselves, at least to any meaningful extent access to necessary supplies. In fact, many of the Dutch forces, as we understood, if they did, in fact, manage to go out on leave, were not allowed to return to resume their responsibilities in helping safeguard the safe area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Who is not allowing them to return?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian forces that had encircled the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And we've talked earlier about the fact -- what your government's view was on who the Serbian forces were composed of. In this case, in terms of when --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, when you talk about Serbian forces, are you talking about -- was your information that they were VRS forces, or VRS forces and VJ forces, or VJ forces?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about both VJ and VRS forces, although certainly it was not possible to ascertain, in any one particular moment, the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you first learned this information from -- I think you said it was Dutch Minister Voorhoeve; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, I'm not sure you may have already stated this: Approximately when was it that you learned about the fact that were forces, apparently, amassing in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was during, in fact, the -- before discussed conference in Paris. I met with several delegation and one of the delegations I met with was the Dutch delegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What month was that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was at the very end of May, very beginning of June. I cannot tell you if it was 31st of May, or 1st or 2nd of June. But it was right then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you received that information, did you discuss it with your government, with president or other officials?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. My stop in Paris was actually coincidental to me returning to Sarajevo to assume the duties of foreign minister. My predecessor had just been killed a few days earlier, and I was summoned to come back as quickly as possible, and I made that brief stop in Paris.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you received that information, did you cause you or anyone in your government any concern?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Frankly, first of all, I found that rather surprising that the Serbian forces would even consider taking over a safe area. I thought that their strategy would be more one of strangulation, that is, a slow process by which, in fact, the population might be driven out, out of necessity. So the idea of something that looked like a full-blown assault was a little bit, even in my mind, unexpected at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you have any views - personally I'm talking about now - as to what may happen in the event of attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: One of the issues in this trial, Your Honour, is the foreseeability of the events at Srebrenica. This gentleman was part of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to the extent that he may have foreseen, given his knowledge base, that may be evidence later on when you're comparing what General Perisic, based on the information he had available to him, ought to have foreseen. So if somebody else who was familiar with the history of Srebrenica and so forth could have foreseen it, then that may be some evidence that you later on you'll consider in adjudicating whether or not General Perisic did and should have foreseen the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you happy, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, not at all, to be perfectly honest. Our position doesn't change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe if you phrase it in neutral terms. Whether it was foreseeable, not just by him but generally speaking, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think I'm going to be, probably, objecting to that too, Your Honour. Then there is some other issues that would -- that arise at that time. I believe that ultimately the question that I believe Ms. Bolton wishes to ask may well be able to be answered, but I don't think we have reached that point yet based on the information that we have in front of us right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I -- I'm sorry, I don't -- I don't understand what you are -- information you [Overlapping speakers] ... I see that we have dealt with a whole lot of history surrounding this area for some time, and I think for me, this question seems to be [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: See there are a variety of problems, not the least of which in the manner that Ms. Bolton has framed her particular proffer. Well, once again, this is not a subject matter that I want to speak of in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, we don't understand, then, the absolute basis because [Overlapping speakers] ... the basis has been established for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm requesting the sound be muted so that I can further amplify my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we mute New York.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] This is the Registrar, Your Honours. Yes, it will be done accordingly now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Just one second, Your Honours. Sorry. I can confirm that the audio has now been muted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. What this witness's personal opinion is, is not relevant, number one, as I said before. Number two, based on the proffer presently made, one of the unique aspects of the testimony that has been adduced from Mr. Sacirbey is that he was privy to information from a variety of sources for which there has been no evidence established that anyone else would have been or could have been specifically, the Central Intelligence Agency, private conversations with various governmental officials, including the Dutch minister, Mr. Voorhoeve. We have also heard information through his testimony that for a considerable period of time there were informal conversations that he was privy to, all of which there is no evidence that General Perisic was privy to. So to equate the two of them, at this time, in the manner that Ms. Bolton has done, is not only, I would submit, not fair for the issue of foreseeability but improper. There is a question that can be asked here, but it is not the question that has been put forth. In addition, if the question is a question of foreseeability then obviously -- I'm not positive that foreseeability in the manner that the Prosecution has been put forth is the issue that will be presented to the Chamber, but if it is, an issue, the issue of foreseeability, the test clearly would be an objective and not a subjective one. And the question as presently propounded requires a subjective response, which is why I rose for the initial time and said that I objected on the grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This question does not equate the witness with General Perisic, maybe the next question may or subsequent questions may do so, but at this stage, we are not at this point. And I think this question is saying, Based on the information you had, what were you able to see the future to look like? Maybe from there, there may be other questions to make it an objective situation. I don't want to sort of even -- I don't even want to couch questions that might make that transition. It is up to the Prosecutor to do so. I'm not sure whether you're say -- do I understand you to be saying that there isn't any sufficient basis for this kind of question to be asked at this objective level? This witness has information in his possession, and I'm sure can he make certain projections based on the information he had. Whether those projections are right or wrong is another matter. And whether those projections could be attributed to anybody else, it is another matter. There would be further evidence required to see -- to check whether any other person would have had that information, because we haven't reached a stage where we are being told that the information he had was also in the possession of Mr. Perisic. So that equation has not been reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand what Your Honour has said. I think that it poses a number of difficulties, not the least of which is that he is being asked to speculate with regard to what could happen in the future, and he is being asked to do that from the standpoint of hindsight. The problem that we have right now with the answer that he could give is we're talking about him prognosticating as to had a would occur, when we know precisely what did occur. There is -- within it, there's a false premise that exists in the first instance, because quite frankly, we all know what the answer will be. And to ask somebody what they thought would happen in the future, after the future has occurred, is, among other things, it's our respective submission, that it's meaningless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response to that part of it, Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, to that part of it, Your Honour, I can indicate that what I'm asking the witness to do is to remember what his thoughts were at the time, what his concerns were at the time; and my friend can cross-examine if he wants to suggest that, in fact, the evidence he gives here today is not, in fact, what he was concerned about at the time, but, in fact, has been influenced by the benefit of hindsight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think we have exhausted the topic sufficiently. We need to rule on this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would request at this time, then, that we go back on to audio so that he can hear us, because that was all done muted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May we please be reconnected with New York via audio. Can you hear us in New York?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We are reconnected. Thank you, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, going back to my question, it was whether you had any -- any views as to what may happen in the event of an attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, Ms. Bolton. Starting with the Drina River valley, places like Visoko, Visegrad, Foca, Bijeljina, going into, particularly, Prijedor where we believe many more thousands of people were murdered, this was all more or less done at the same military and political leadership and that continued through much of the war, of course, with the greater intensity during the beginning of the war. But it was from our perspective, that is the perspective of the mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and from my conversations with President Izetbegovic and other Bosnian leaders, it was a very really possibility that three individuals, not only would be expelled, but, in fact, could be massacred.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How were you expecting the United Nations forces in Srebrenica to react to the use of military forces by the Bosnian -- or the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We actually expected the UN forces along with the support of NATO, which was critical, to confront any forces that would attack the safe areas, especially keeping in the mind the evidence we discussed already regarding how much effort went into defining the safe areas and defining what the mandate was in defending those safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How soon after the offensive began did you start to receive reports as to what was happening in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I think I need to be asking you to clarify. The offensive seemed to start really quite -- months before the actually takeover of the enclave, but the most urgent period seemed to be only a few days before the enclave actually fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could deal with the beginning of July 1995 and the shelling at Srebrenica, sorry, sir. How soon after the -- sorry, first, was there -- were you aware of a period of intense shelling in the beginning of July 1995, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first situation I became aware of, having returned to Sarajevo from Paris, was a visit from the delegation of Srebrenica that was visiting President Izetbegovic. He called me in to meet with them, and they were emphasizing two things, that, in fact, the military action had intensified, but, in fact, the humanitarian action was at the point of being highly dramatic, in fact, life threatening. When, in fact, I left Sarajevo at that time, I was instructed by President Izetbegovic, once again, to ensure airdrops or any other means that, in fact, the enclave could receive necessities of life; and, of course, I was told to do whatever would be necessary to try to protect the enclave from military attack. The first really information of the intensified military attack that I received actually came when I was in The Hague. And it was in conjunction with also Dutch officials who were receiving similar information, and this was the few days right before the enclave actually was overrun. The attacks were intensive, and most importantly, there was this sense that the military forces that had been recently introduced or reinforced, if you would, were tightening the noose, to use that term.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you started to receive those kinds of reports, did you make any efforts to bring that information to the attention of the United Nations Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did through our mission in New York. But also through contacts with the UN officials on the ground in Bosnia and, of course, through my Dutch colleagues, the foreign ministry, van Mierlo, and the Dutch defence minister, Voorhoeve. We had several meetings including their -- some of their military staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask you to turn to tab 12 in the binder you have in front of you, sir, and that's 65 ter 8863.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Should be a letter from your charge d'affaires, 9th July, 1995 with an annex written by yourself on that same date.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could you confirm, sir, that this is a true copy of the letter that you sent to the Security Council on July 9th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph, you appear to be requesting an emergency session of the Security Council, to address the events in Srebrenica. Did that emergency --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did that emergency session take place?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have called it. I would not have been present there. I believe it did take place, though, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be tendered as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2498.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you turn, please, sir, to tab 17 in your binder; 65 ter 8866.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm there, Ms. Bolton. I realize that my answer may have been incomplete to one of your previous questions, and just for the record, I would like to be very complete on that. Besides people and institutions contacted regarding the attack on Srebrenica, I also contacted NATO and NATO member states, because Srebrenica was also a NATO - what was then called a protected zone - and it was, in fact, NATO that would also be called upon, in particular, with its resources the safe area/protected zone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Dealing with the document in front of you, sir, it appears to be a letter dated 13th July, 1995, from Mr. Misic. And in the first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The first paragraph he alludes to reports from the Srebrenica area communicated to our government: "Serb forces have begun to separate boys and men, aged 13 and older." Later in that paragraph he indicates: "According to reports from this area, a number of trucks with detained men may have been taken to unknown destinations. The fate of these detainees is uncertain, and there are substantial grounds to fear their execution, those these reports could not yet be confirmed." And he then states: "These acts constitute grave violations of the Geneva Conventions and the norms of international humanitarian law and must be responded to in the strongest terms." First of all, can you authenticate this letter sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It was sent -- the letterhead indicates General Assembly and Security Council. What does that mean in terms -- and then, sorry, the last paragraph indicates they want it circulated, Mr. Misic wanted it circulated as a document of the General Assembly under items 28 and 114 C of the preliminary list and of the Security Council. What would that mean in terms of circulation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course the matter was under consideration by the Security Council and also by that time for several years then there had been an agenda item titled the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This -- this document, therefore, would have been circulated to all member states as well as the FRY and, of course, observer missions as a document both of the General Assembly and the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What would that mean in terms of whether the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's representatives at the United Nations would have been entitled to receive it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that question has answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would have been entitled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It says they did actually circulate -- it was circulated to them. Look at the previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I'm getting tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. It's late in the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The next document, sir, that I would like to deal with is a document that would require us to move in closed session. I'm in Your Honours hands as to whether you wish to break five minutes early or try to go with this document in the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you are able to finish in the next five minutes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Brief indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I forgot to move a tab, the last document we were just discussing admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 8866 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2499.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What I'm going to suggest, Your Honour, is the next document is one that I anticipate the witness would need a little bit of time to read. So if we could perhaps -- I don't think I can deal with in five minutes, as a result, if we could, perhaps, ask the Registrar to allow him to read it, maybe, before we start the session tomorrow morning. Then I could ask my questions of him at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see, Mr. Guy-Smith. I see you shaking your head, sir ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am uncomfortable with it, but I will allow it. I'll not the person to allow it. I'm uncomfortable with it, but if that is what the Chamber wishes to do, I'll -- I'm in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, I think I shouldn't allow it, for the simple reason that the witness is not supposed to discuss the case with anyone else during adjournments.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's a good point, Your Honour. Then I think I have gone as far as I can for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take an adjournment until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of June, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
